items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

items.reference: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.

items.reference: Chapter Four: The Last Map. There is a map in the British Library that is wrong in a way that can only be described as deliberately wrong. It was drawn in 1602 by a cartographer whose name has been lost, which is itself suspicious, since cartographers of that period were meticulous about attribution. The map shows the eastern coast of an island that does not exist. The island is rendered in extraordinary detail — bays, inlets, a river that curves south before turning back on itself, a mountain with a notation in Latin that translates, roughly, as 'here the light is different.' On the reverse side of the map, in a hand that appears to be different from the cartographer's, someone has written: 'I have been here.' Dr. Evelyn Cross had been studying this map for eleven years. She had examined it under ultraviolet light, under infrared imaging, under a microscope powerful enough to count the individual fibres of the vellum. She had traced the coastline against every known island in every ocean and found nothing. She had run the Latin text through six different translation tools and received six slightly different answers, all of which agreed on 'light' and disagreed on everything else. Today, for reasons she couldn't fully explain, she thought she was close.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Lesson 4: Understanding the Water Cycle. Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle — from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapour — a gas — and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapour rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapour condenses — meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude — that's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation — which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. And some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

items.reference: Pre-Procedure Instructions: Upper GI Endoscopy. Your upper endoscopy is scheduled for Wednesday the 22nd at 9:30 AM at City General Hospital, Endoscopy Suite, Level 3. Diet: You must have nothing to eat for at least six hours before your procedure. You may drink clear fluids — water, black tea, black coffee, apple juice, or clear broth — up to two hours before your appointment. Do not drink milk or eat any solid food after midnight the night before. Medications: Take all regular medications as usual with a small sip of water on the morning of your procedure, unless your doctor has specifically told you otherwise. If you take blood-thinning medications such as warfarin, clopidogrel, or aspirin, please contact us at least five days before your appointment as you may need to temporarily stop these. If you take insulin, do not take your morning dose — contact your diabetes team for guidance. Arrival: Please arrive 30 minutes before your scheduled time to allow for registration and preparation. Bring a list of your current medications, your hospital card, and any previous endoscopy reports if you have them. After the procedure: You will be in recovery for approximately 45 minutes while the sedation wears off. You must have a responsible adult available to take you home — you cannot travel by taxi or public transport alone, and you must not drive for 24 hours. You may feel bloated or gassy for a few hours after the procedure — this is normal.

items.reference: There is a village in the western Highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was A' Chomraich — meaning the sanctuary. In the eighth century a monk called Maelrubha came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This right of sanctuary held for a thousand years, and was still recognised into the seventeenth century, when Highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather — the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way — something of the sanctuary is still there, waiting for the traveller who thinks they have arrived, and finds instead that they have been received.

items.reference: Earnings Call Summary: TechCorp Inc., Q1 2026. Revenue: $14.2 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year and $400 million ahead of analyst consensus of $13.8 billion. This was the fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth. Earnings per share: $2.84 diluted, compared to consensus of $2.61 and $2.31 in Q1 2025. This represents a 23 percent increase year-over-year. Gross margin: 42.3 percent, expanding 1.4 percentage points compared to the same quarter last year, driven by a higher mix of software and services revenue, which carry margins above 60 percent. Cloud segment: revenue of $6.1 billion, up 31 percent year-over-year, representing 43 percent of total revenue. Operating income from cloud was $1.8 billion, a margin of 29.5 percent. Guidance for Q2 2026: the company guided for revenue of $14.6 billion to $15 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 16 to 19 percent. Earnings per share guidance of $2.90 to $3.05 was ahead of current analyst consensus of $2.76. Management commentary: CEO Michael Chen said growth was broad-based across all segments and geographies, with particularly strong performance in enterprise AI tools, which now represent 12 percent of total revenue, up from 4 percent a year ago. The company announced a $5 billion share repurchase programme and raised its quarterly dividend by 8 percent to $0.52 per share.

items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

items.reference: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Chapter Four: The Last Map. There is a map in the British Library that is wrong in a way that can only be described as deliberately wrong. It was drawn in 1602 by a cartographer whose name has been lost, which is itself suspicious, since cartographers of that period were meticulous about attribution. The map shows the eastern coast of an island that does not exist. The island is rendered in extraordinary detail — bays, inlets, a river that curves south before turning back on itself, a mountain with a notation in Latin that translates, roughly, as 'here the light is different.' On the reverse side of the map, in a hand that appears to be different from the cartographer's, someone has written: 'I have been here.' Dr. Evelyn Cross had been studying this map for eleven years. She had examined it under ultraviolet light, under infrared imaging, under a microscope powerful enough to count the individual fibres of the vellum. She had traced the coastline against every known island in every ocean and found nothing. She had run the Latin text through six different translation tools and received six slightly different answers, all of which agreed on 'light' and disagreed on everything else. Today, for reasons she couldn't fully explain, she thought she was close.

items.reference: Lesson 4: Understanding the Water Cycle. Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle — from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapour — a gas — and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapour rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapour condenses — meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude — that's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation — which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. And some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapor rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapor condenses, meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude. That's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation, which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail, depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams, and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater, and some of it falls as snow on high mountains, and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

items.reference: There is a village in the western Highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was A' Chomraich — meaning the sanctuary. In the eighth century a monk called Maelrubha came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This right of sanctuary held for a thousand years, and was still recognised into the seventeenth century, when Highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather — the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way — something of the sanctuary is still there, waiting for the traveller who thinks they have arrived, and finds instead that they have been received.

items.reference: Earnings Call Summary: TechCorp Inc., Q1 2026. Revenue: $14.2 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year and $400 million ahead of analyst consensus of $13.8 billion. This was the fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth. Earnings per share: $2.84 diluted, compared to consensus of $2.61 and $2.31 in Q1 2025. This represents a 23 percent increase year-over-year. Gross margin: 42.3 percent, expanding 1.4 percentage points compared to the same quarter last year, driven by a higher mix of software and services revenue, which carry margins above 60 percent. Cloud segment: revenue of $6.1 billion, up 31 percent year-over-year, representing 43 percent of total revenue. Operating income from cloud was $1.8 billion, a margin of 29.5 percent. Guidance for Q2 2026: the company guided for revenue of $14.6 billion to $15 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 16 to 19 percent. Earnings per share guidance of $2.90 to $3.05 was ahead of current analyst consensus of $2.76. Management commentary: CEO Michael Chen said growth was broad-based across all segments and geographies, with particularly strong performance in enterprise AI tools, which now represent 12 percent of total revenue, up from 4 percent a year ago. The company announced a $5 billion share repurchase programme and raised its quarterly dividend by 8 percent to $0.52 per share.

items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

items.reference: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.

items.reference: Chapter Four: The Last Map. There is a map in the British Library that is wrong in a way that can only be described as deliberately wrong. It was drawn in 1602 by a cartographer whose name has been lost, which is itself suspicious, since cartographers of that period were meticulous about attribution. The map shows the eastern coast of an island that does not exist. The island is rendered in extraordinary detail — bays, inlets, a river that curves south before turning back on itself, a mountain with a notation in Latin that translates, roughly, as 'here the light is different.' On the reverse side of the map, in a hand that appears to be different from the cartographer's, someone has written: 'I have been here.' Dr. Evelyn Cross had been studying this map for eleven years. She had examined it under ultraviolet light, under infrared imaging, under a microscope powerful enough to count the individual fibres of the vellum. She had traced the coastline against every known island in every ocean and found nothing. She had run the Latin text through six different translation tools and received six slightly different answers, all of which agreed on 'light' and disagreed on everything else. Today, for reasons she couldn't fully explain, she thought she was close.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the Shadow Chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67% over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support, but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending, for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Lesson 4: Understanding the Water Cycle. Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle — from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapour — a gas — and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapour rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapour condenses — meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude — that's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation — which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. And some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

items.reference: There is a village in the western Highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was A' Chomraich — meaning the sanctuary. In the eighth century a monk called Maelrubha came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This right of sanctuary held for a thousand years, and was still recognised into the seventeenth century, when Highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather — the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way — something of the sanctuary is still there, waiting for the traveller who thinks they have arrived, and finds instead that they have been received.

items.reference: Earnings Call Summary: TechCorp Inc., Q1 2026. Revenue: $14.2 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year and $400 million ahead of analyst consensus of $13.8 billion. This was the fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth. Earnings per share: $2.84 diluted, compared to consensus of $2.61 and $2.31 in Q1 2025. This represents a 23 percent increase year-over-year. Gross margin: 42.3 percent, expanding 1.4 percentage points compared to the same quarter last year, driven by a higher mix of software and services revenue, which carry margins above 60 percent. Cloud segment: revenue of $6.1 billion, up 31 percent year-over-year, representing 43 percent of total revenue. Operating income from cloud was $1.8 billion, a margin of 29.5 percent. Guidance for Q2 2026: the company guided for revenue of $14.6 billion to $15 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 16 to 19 percent. Earnings per share guidance of $2.90 to $3.05 was ahead of current analyst consensus of $2.76. Management commentary: CEO Michael Chen said growth was broad-based across all segments and geographies, with particularly strong performance in enterprise AI tools, which now represent 12 percent of total revenue, up from 4 percent a year ago. The company announced a $5 billion share repurchase programme and raised its quarterly dividend by 8 percent to $0.52 per share.

items.reference: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.

items.reference: Chapter Four: The Last Map. There is a map in the British Library that is wrong in a way that can only be described as deliberately wrong. It was drawn in 1602 by a cartographer whose name has been lost, which is itself suspicious, since cartographers of that period were meticulous about attribution. The map shows the eastern coast of an island that does not exist. The island is rendered in extraordinary detail — bays, inlets, a river that curves south before turning back on itself, a mountain with a notation in Latin that translates, roughly, as 'here the light is different.' On the reverse side of the map, in a hand that appears to be different from the cartographer's, someone has written: 'I have been here.' Dr. Evelyn Cross had been studying this map for eleven years. She had examined it under ultraviolet light, under infrared imaging, under a microscope powerful enough to count the individual fibres of the vellum. She had traced the coastline against every known island in every ocean and found nothing. She had run the Latin text through six different translation tools and received six slightly different answers, all of which agreed on 'light' and disagreed on everything else. Today, for reasons she couldn't fully explain, she thought she was close.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Lesson 4: Understanding the Water Cycle. Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle — from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapour — a gas — and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapour rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapour condenses — meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude — that's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation — which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. And some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

items.reference: Pre-Procedure Instructions: Upper GI Endoscopy. Your upper endoscopy is scheduled for Wednesday the 22nd at 9:30 AM at City General Hospital, Endoscopy Suite, Level 3. Diet: You must have nothing to eat for at least six hours before your procedure. You may drink clear fluids — water, black tea, black coffee, apple juice, or clear broth — up to two hours before your appointment. Do not drink milk or eat any solid food after midnight the night before. Medications: Take all regular medications as usual with a small sip of water on the morning of your procedure, unless your doctor has specifically told you otherwise. If you take blood-thinning medications such as warfarin, clopidogrel, or aspirin, please contact us at least five days before your appointment as you may need to temporarily stop these. If you take insulin, do not take your morning dose — contact your diabetes team for guidance. Arrival: Please arrive 30 minutes before your scheduled time to allow for registration and preparation. Bring a list of your current medications, your hospital card, and any previous endoscopy reports if you have them. After the procedure: You will be in recovery for approximately 45 minutes while the sedation wears off. You must have a responsible adult available to take you home — you cannot travel by taxi or public transport alone, and you must not drive for 24 hours. You may feel bloated or gassy for a few hours after the procedure — this is normal.

items.reference: Earnings Call Summary: TechCorp Inc., Q1 2026. Revenue: $14.2 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year and $400 million ahead of analyst consensus of $13.8 billion. This was the fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth. Earnings per share: $2.84 diluted, compared to consensus of $2.61 and $2.31 in Q1 2025. This represents a 23 percent increase year-over-year. Gross margin: 42.3 percent, expanding 1.4 percentage points compared to the same quarter last year, driven by a higher mix of software and services revenue, which carry margins above 60 percent. Cloud segment: revenue of $6.1 billion, up 31 percent year-over-year, representing 43 percent of total revenue. Operating income from cloud was $1.8 billion, a margin of 29.5 percent. Guidance for Q2 2026: the company guided for revenue of $14.6 billion to $15 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 16 to 19 percent. Earnings per share guidance of $2.90 to $3.05 was ahead of current analyst consensus of $2.76. Management commentary: CEO Michael Chen said growth was broad-based across all segments and geographies, with particularly strong performance in enterprise AI tools, which now represent 12 percent of total revenue, up from 4 percent a year ago. The company announced a $5 billion share repurchase programme and raised its quarterly dividend by 8 percent to $0.52 per share.

items.reference: There is a village in the western Highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was A' Chomraich — meaning the sanctuary. In the eighth century a monk called Maelrubha came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This right of sanctuary held for a thousand years, and was still recognised into the seventeenth century, when Highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather — the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way — something of the sanctuary is still there, waiting for the traveller who thinks they have arrived, and finds instead that they have been received.

items.whisper: There is a village in the western highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was a cumraich, meaning the sanctuary. In the 8th century a monk called Malruba came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This rite of sanctuary held for a thousand years and was still recognized into the 17th century when highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather, the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way, something of this sanctuary is still there waiting for the traveler who thinks they have arrived and finds instead that they have been received.

items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'll help you get back in, but I do need to walk through our identity verification carefully — this is exactly the situation attackers try to exploit, so please bear with me. Can you confirm the email address on the account for me? And can you tell me the last four digits of the payment method we have on file? Okay, that matches. Now, we need to establish that the person on this call is the account holder rather than someone with the email and card details. I'm going to ask two questions from your account history that only you should be able to answer. First: what city was the account originally registered from? And second: what was the approximate amount of your most recent completed transaction, within five dollars? Both correct. Thank you for going through that. What I'm going to do now is reset your two-factor device pairing rather than the password itself — you'll receive a verification email and, once you click it, you'll be prompted to enrol a new authenticator. Once that's done, your existing password will still work; if you'd prefer to change it as well, you can do so from account settings after logging in. The reset email will arrive within five minutes. If it doesn't, check your spam folder, and if it's still not there, call us back and reference case number SEC-9917-42.

items.reference: I'm really sorry about the cancellation — I know that's the last thing you need on a Sunday evening. Let me pull up your booking. I see reference JXQ4T2, flight 447 from Manchester to Malaga, originally departing at seven-fifteen tomorrow morning. That's been cancelled, and I have three options I can offer you. The first is our nine-forty flight tomorrow morning, same route, seats in economy and one exit-row seat available. The second is a rerouting through Barcelona, leaving at six a.m., landing you in Malaga just after two in the afternoon — longer travel time but no risk of being bumped, since both legs are already ticketed. The third option is a next-day departure, direct at seven-thirty on Tuesday morning, with hotel accommodation and meal vouchers provided by us at no charge if the delay of a day is too disruptive. If you're travelling on a fixed schedule and same-day matters, I'd recommend the nine-forty — you'd land only about two hours later than originally planned. Which would work best for you? I've moved you to the nine-forty. Your new boarding pass will be issued to the app automatically, and you'll need to be at the gate no later than nine-ten. If you'd like, I can also arrange a small compensation credit for the disruption — it's a hundred and twenty euros in travel credit, valid for twelve months. Is that useful?

items.reference: Chapter Four: The Last Map. There is a map in the British Library that is wrong in a way that can only be described as deliberately wrong. It was drawn in 1602 by a cartographer whose name has been lost, which is itself suspicious, since cartographers of that period were meticulous about attribution. The map shows the eastern coast of an island that does not exist. The island is rendered in extraordinary detail — bays, inlets, a river that curves south before turning back on itself, a mountain with a notation in Latin that translates, roughly, as 'here the light is different.' On the reverse side of the map, in a hand that appears to be different from the cartographer's, someone has written: 'I have been here.' Dr. Evelyn Cross had been studying this map for eleven years. She had examined it under ultraviolet light, under infrared imaging, under a microscope powerful enough to count the individual fibres of the vellum. She had traced the coastline against every known island in every ocean and found nothing. She had run the Latin text through six different translation tools and received six slightly different answers, all of which agreed on 'light' and disagreed on everything else. Today, for reasons she couldn't fully explain, she thought she was close.

items.reference: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Pre-Procedure Instructions: Upper GI Endoscopy. Your upper endoscopy is scheduled for Wednesday the 22nd at 9:30 AM at City General Hospital, Endoscopy Suite, Level 3. Diet: You must have nothing to eat for at least six hours before your procedure. You may drink clear fluids — water, black tea, black coffee, apple juice, or clear broth — up to two hours before your appointment. Do not drink milk or eat any solid food after midnight the night before. Medications: Take all regular medications as usual with a small sip of water on the morning of your procedure, unless your doctor has specifically told you otherwise. If you take blood-thinning medications such as warfarin, clopidogrel, or aspirin, please contact us at least five days before your appointment as you may need to temporarily stop these. If you take insulin, do not take your morning dose — contact your diabetes team for guidance. Arrival: Please arrive 30 minutes before your scheduled time to allow for registration and preparation. Bring a list of your current medications, your hospital card, and any previous endoscopy reports if you have them. After the procedure: You will be in recovery for approximately 45 minutes while the sedation wears off. You must have a responsible adult available to take you home — you cannot travel by taxi or public transport alone, and you must not drive for 24 hours. You may feel bloated or gassy for a few hours after the procedure — this is normal.

items.reference: Lesson 4: Understanding the Water Cycle. Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle — from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapour — a gas — and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapour rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapour condenses — meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude — that's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation — which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. And some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

items.reference: There is a village in the western Highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was A' Chomraich — meaning the sanctuary. In the eighth century a monk called Maelrubha came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This right of sanctuary held for a thousand years, and was still recognised into the seventeenth century, when Highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather — the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way — something of the sanctuary is still there, waiting for the traveller who thinks they have arrived, and finds instead that they have been received.

items.reference: Earnings Call Summary: TechCorp Inc., Q1 2026. Revenue: $14.2 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year and $400 million ahead of analyst consensus of $13.8 billion. This was the fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth. Earnings per share: $2.84 diluted, compared to consensus of $2.61 and $2.31 in Q1 2025. This represents a 23 percent increase year-over-year. Gross margin: 42.3 percent, expanding 1.4 percentage points compared to the same quarter last year, driven by a higher mix of software and services revenue, which carry margins above 60 percent. Cloud segment: revenue of $6.1 billion, up 31 percent year-over-year, representing 43 percent of total revenue. Operating income from cloud was $1.8 billion, a margin of 29.5 percent. Guidance for Q2 2026: the company guided for revenue of $14.6 billion to $15 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 16 to 19 percent. Earnings per share guidance of $2.90 to $3.05 was ahead of current analyst consensus of $2.76. Management commentary: CEO Michael Chen said growth was broad-based across all segments and geographies, with particularly strong performance in enterprise AI tools, which now represent 12 percent of total revenue, up from 4 percent a year ago. The company announced a $5 billion share repurchase programme and raised its quarterly dividend by 8 percent to $0.52 per share.

items.reference: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.

items.reference: Chapter Four: The Last Map. There is a map in the British Library that is wrong in a way that can only be described as deliberately wrong. It was drawn in 1602 by a cartographer whose name has been lost, which is itself suspicious, since cartographers of that period were meticulous about attribution. The map shows the eastern coast of an island that does not exist. The island is rendered in extraordinary detail — bays, inlets, a river that curves south before turning back on itself, a mountain with a notation in Latin that translates, roughly, as 'here the light is different.' On the reverse side of the map, in a hand that appears to be different from the cartographer's, someone has written: 'I have been here.' Dr. Evelyn Cross had been studying this map for eleven years. She had examined it under ultraviolet light, under infrared imaging, under a microscope powerful enough to count the individual fibres of the vellum. She had traced the coastline against every known island in every ocean and found nothing. She had run the Latin text through six different translation tools and received six slightly different answers, all of which agreed on 'light' and disagreed on everything else. Today, for reasons she couldn't fully explain, she thought she was close.

items.reference: Lesson 4: Understanding the Water Cycle. Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle — from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapour — a gas — and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapour rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapour condenses — meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude — that's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation — which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. And some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

items.reference: There is a village in the western Highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was A' Chomraich — meaning the sanctuary. In the eighth century a monk called Maelrubha came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This right of sanctuary held for a thousand years, and was still recognised into the seventeenth century, when Highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather — the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way — something of the sanctuary is still there, waiting for the traveller who thinks they have arrived, and finds instead that they have been received.

items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

You can print it at home or take the barcode to any drop-off location; we've got about four thousand of them across the country, so there should be one close to you. You don't need to package it in the original box, but do please include the original invoice or a note with your order number. On the exchange side, I've reserved a medium in the same colour and style, and I'm going to expedite the shipping so it arrives before you send the large back. That way you're not waiting. You should see the medium delivered within two business days. The system will automatically match the return to the exchange, so you won't be charged again — but if you do see a pending charge on your account before the return processes, it'll fall off within about a week. Is there anything else about this order I should look at, or is there anything else I can help you with today?

items.reference: First of all, I'm sorry to hear about the accident — I hope you and everyone involved are okay. Take your time. I'm going to walk you through what we need to get a claim opened, but there's no rush. When you're ready, could you tell me the date and approximate time of the incident? Okay, Sunday afternoon around four. And where did it happen — I don't need the exact address if you don't have it, just the road or the nearest intersection. The junction of Elm Street and Fourth Avenue, got it. Was anyone injured, either in your vehicle or the other vehicle? I'm glad to hear it. Now, do you have the other driver's insurance information — company name, policy number, and their contact details? If not, that's fine, we can request it through the exchange process. And did the police attend the scene? If they did, was a report number issued? Perfect, I've noted case number seven-two-two-nine-eight from Metro Police. I have enough now to open your claim under file number CL-2026-8734. Your assigned adjuster will call you within one business day. In the meantime, if you have photographs of the vehicles or the scene, please email them to claims@example.com with your file number in the subject line. Do not have your vehicle repaired before speaking to the adjuster, unless it's a safety issue — is there anything about the current condition that can't wait?

items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand you're locked out of your account and the reset link isn't reaching your two-factor device. I'll help you get back in, but I do need to walk through our identity verification carefully — this is exactly the situation attackers try to exploit, so please bear with me. Can you confirm the email address on the account for me? And can you tell me the last four digits of the payment method we have on file? Okay, that matches. Now, we need to establish that the person on this call is the account holder rather than someone with the email and card details. I'm going to ask two questions from your account history that only you should be able to answer. First: what city was the account originally registered from? And second: what was the approximate amount of your most recent completed transaction, within five dollars? Both correct. Thank you for going through that. What I'm going to do now is reset your two-factor device pairing rather than the password itself — you'll receive a verification email and, once you click it, you'll be prompted to enrol a new authenticator. Once that's done, your existing password will still work; if you'd prefer to change it as well, you can do so from account settings after logging in. The reset email will arrive within five minutes. If it doesn't, check your spam folder, and if it's still not there, call us back and reference case number SEC-9917-42.

items.reference: I'm really sorry about the cancellation — I know that's the last thing you need on a Sunday evening. Let me pull up your booking. I see reference JXQ4T2, flight 447 from Manchester to Malaga, originally departing at seven-fifteen tomorrow morning. That's been cancelled, and I have three options I can offer you. The first is our nine-forty flight tomorrow morning, same route, seats in economy and one exit-row seat available. The second is a rerouting through Barcelona, leaving at six a.m., landing you in Malaga just after two in the afternoon — longer travel time but no risk of being bumped, since both legs are already ticketed. The third option is a next-day departure, direct at seven-thirty on Tuesday morning, with hotel accommodation and meal vouchers provided by us at no charge if the delay of a day is too disruptive. If you're travelling on a fixed schedule and same-day matters, I'd recommend the nine-forty — you'd land only about two hours later than originally planned. Which would work best for you? I've moved you to the nine-forty. Your new boarding pass will be issued to the app automatically, and you'll need to be at the gate no later than nine-ten. If you'd like, I can also arrange a small compensation credit for the disruption — it's a hundred and twenty euros in travel credit, valid for twelve months. Is that useful?

items.reference: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.

items.reference: Chapter Four: The Last Map. There is a map in the British Library that is wrong in a way that can only be described as deliberately wrong. It was drawn in 1602 by a cartographer whose name has been lost, which is itself suspicious, since cartographers of that period were meticulous about attribution. The map shows the eastern coast of an island that does not exist. The island is rendered in extraordinary detail — bays, inlets, a river that curves south before turning back on itself, a mountain with a notation in Latin that translates, roughly, as 'here the light is different.' On the reverse side of the map, in a hand that appears to be different from the cartographer's, someone has written: 'I have been here.' Dr. Evelyn Cross had been studying this map for eleven years. She had examined it under ultraviolet light, under infrared imaging, under a microscope powerful enough to count the individual fibres of the vellum. She had traced the coastline against every known island in every ocean and found nothing. She had run the Latin text through six different translation tools and received six slightly different answers, all of which agreed on 'light' and disagreed on everything else. Today, for reasons she couldn't fully explain, she thought she was close.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Lesson 4: Understanding the Water Cycle. Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle — from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapour — a gas — and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapour rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapour condenses — meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude — that's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation — which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. And some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

items.whisper: Lesson 4. Understanding the Water Cycle Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle, from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapor, a gas, and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapor rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapor condenses, meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude. That's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation, which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail, depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams, and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater, and some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

items.reference: Earnings Call Summary: TechCorp Inc., Q1 2026. Revenue: $14.2 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year and $400 million ahead of analyst consensus of $13.8 billion. Cloud segment: revenue of $6.1 billion, up 31 percent year-over-year, representing 43 percent of total revenue. Operating income from cloud was $1.8 billion, a margin of 29.5 percent. The company announced a $5 billion share repurchase programme and raised its quarterly dividend by 8 percent to $0.52 per share.

items.reference: There is a village in the western Highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was A' Chomraich — meaning the sanctuary. In the eighth century a monk called Maelrubha came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This right of sanctuary held for a thousand years, and was still recognised into the seventeenth century, when Highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather — the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way — something of the sanctuary is still there, waiting for the traveller who thinks they have arrived, and finds instead that they have been received.

items.reference: I understand you've been waiting on hold and I appreciate your patience. Let me make sure I have everything I need to resolve this for you today so you don't have to call back. You're asking about the double charge on your account from the 15th. I can see two transactions here — one for $42.50 and another for $42.50 posted eight minutes apart. That does look like a duplicate. What likely happened is that the payment page timed out on your end and the request was submitted twice before the system caught it. I'm going to reverse the second charge now. The reversal will show as a pending credit within 24 hours and the funds will fully clear in three to five business days depending on your bank. I'd also recommend checking if your bank placed a hold — sometimes both charges remain visible during processing even after we've reversed one on our end. I'm also going to add a note to your account so that if you call back and the credit hasn't appeared by Friday, the next agent can escalate it directly to our payments team without you needing to explain everything again. items.reference: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.

The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret? Well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was 40 miles away, which was part of what made it strange.
